sentenceSets.sentence: The chair convoked an emergency session when it became clear the regular meeting could not address the crisis.

answerChoices.reasoning: The sentence makes the chair the one issuing the call while the session is the thing brought into being; 'convened' more often describes a body coming together on its own timetable, which clashes with the picture of an authority reaching for an unscheduled session.
What follows the blank is a session, not people; 'summoned' fits ordering individuals to appear and reads oddly when its object is the meeting itself.
'Assembled' describes physically bringing bodies into one room, but the sentence is about the formal act of putting an extra session on the books because the regular one was inadequate.
The phrase 'when it became clear' marks an immediate response to an unfolding crisis, while scheduling implies fixing something for a later date rather than getting people into the room now.
The sentence already identifies the person as the chair, so presiding over the session tells us nothing new; the point being made is that the extra session came into existence at all.
Attending is passive participation, but the sentence credits this person with the initiative taken once the regular meeting proved inadequate.
Announcing is publicity about a session that already exists; the sentence describes the act that brought the session about in response to the crisis.
A request can be refused, which sits badly with a chair acting decisively in a crisis and with a session that plainly took place.
Adjourning ends a sitting, the opposite of what the sentence describes happening because the regular meeting was insufficient.
Canceling would leave the crisis unaddressed, contradicting the stated reason for acting.
Dissolving disbands a body permanently, which makes no sense as a response to needing more meeting time.

sentenceSets.sentence: When the treaty talks stalled, the archbishop convoked the regional synod at short notice, and delegates arrived from three provinces within the week.

answerChoices.reasoning: 'Gathered' suggests collecting people already nearby, yet the delegates had to travel in from three provinces after being sent for, which points to a formal call rather than a rounding-up.
Mustering carries a military flavor of drawing up forces for action; the object here is a deliberative church assembly convened to take up stalled talks.
Rallying implies stirring up enthusiasm for a cause, but nothing in the sentence describes persuasion — only a summons that delegates answered within the week.
Marshaling is about arranging and organizing resources already at hand, which does not match a body that had to be called into existence before its members could travel.
Notification is merely informing; the sentence shows an authority whose word actually brought delegates across provincial borders.
Petitioning would make the archbishop a supplicant, but the sentence presents him as the one with power to act when the talks stalled.
Hosting concerns accommodating a gathering, not the decisive act taken at short notice that caused the gathering to occur.
Addressing a synod presupposes that the synod is already sitting, whereas the delegates only arrive in the week following this act.
Disbanding would send the delegates home, contradicting their arrival from three provinces.
Postponement conflicts directly with 'at short notice' and with delegates showing up within the week.
Ignoring the synod cannot produce the travel and attendance the second half of the sentence records.

sentenceSets.sentence: Rather than convoke the full committee over a single line of text, the editor settled the dispute by email.

answerChoices.reasoning: 'Call' alone is vague about what is being called and is more naturally completed by 'call a meeting of'; the contrast drawn is between formally bringing the whole body into session and a quiet exchange of messages.
Reconvening implies resuming a session already begun and adjourned, but nothing suggests the committee had been sitting on this line of text before.
Consulting the committee could be done by the very email the editor chose, so it fails to provide the contrast the sentence sets up between two different procedures.
Canvassing means soliciting opinions one by one, which is closer to what the editor actually did than to the cumbersome alternative being rejected.
Alerting the committee is compatible with settling things by email and so is not the burdensome option the sentence contrasts with.
'Involve' is too general to be the thing avoided, since sending an email about the dispute already involves someone.
A survey is a way of collecting views remotely, precisely the sort of thing email handles, so it cannot be the heavy procedure being skipped.
Lobbying means pressing members to adopt a position, but the editor is described as resolving the matter, not campaigning within it.
Dismissing the committee is a matter of removing it from office, unrelated to choosing a lighter way to resolve a small textual argument.
'Rather than avoid the full committee' reverses the logic, since avoiding the committee is exactly what the editor did.
Abolishing a committee over one line of text is a wildly disproportionate act and has nothing to do with the email solution described.
